metadata.review_status: DRAFT - not yet reviewed by an agricultural expert
metadata.source_verification: Each source URL was fetched and its content checked for the named disease on 2026-11-03. Practices are paraphrased from those pages; source tags in parentheses show which source states each item. Doses, rates, spray intervals and pre-harvest intervals were deliberately NOT recorded. Raw research records are in treatment/research/.
metadata.regional_note: Indian sources (TNAU Agritech Portal, Punjab Agricultural University) were used where a page for the disease was found. ICAR institute websites could not be reached from the build environment, so most sources are US land-grant university extension services. Recommendations and active ingredients must be checked against ICAR / State Agricultural University packages of practices and CIB&RC label claims before use in India.

schema.pathogen_type: fungal | oomycete | bacterial | viral | arthropod_pest | none
schema.management: severity-independent management (systemic diseases: viral, HLB, esca)
schema.chemical_guidance: generic statements + active ingredients named by the cited source; never doses

disclaimer: Advisory decision support only - not a prescription. The diagnosis comes from an image classifier trained on laboratory images (PlantVillage) and can be wrong; the severity value is an experimental colour-segmentation estimate. Guidance is summarised from the cited extension sources, has not yet been reviewed by an agricultural expert, and may not suit your region, crop stage or local regulations. Always follow the product label and the advice of your local agricultural officer or Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK).

decision_rules.description: healthy -> preventive only; confidence < threshold -> no disease-specific or chemical advice; systemic diseases -> no curative chemical, removal + vector management; mild -> cultural + monitoring; moderate -> + disease-specific management and generic chemical guidance; severe -> + removal of heavily infected material + expert consultation; severity unknown -> moderate-level guidance + field inspection.

messages.low_confidence: The model is not confident about this identification. Disease-specific and chemical advice is withheld. Retake the photo (one leaf, plain background, even light) or ask an agricultural extension officer / KVK to confirm the diagnosis.
messages.low_confidence_healthy: The leaf was classified as healthy, but with low confidence. If you can see symptoms, retake the photo or ask an expert.
messages.unknown_disease: This class is not in the treatment knowledge base, so no specific guidance can be given. Consult an agricultural expert.
messages.severity_unknown: Severity could not be measured reliably from this image. Base management decisions on a field inspection of how much of the crop is affected.
messages.chemical_not_indicated_healthy: No treatment is indicated for a healthy leaf.
messages.chemical_not_indicated_mild: At mild severity this system recommends cultural practices and close monitoring first. If symptoms spread, re-assess or consult an expert before considering chemical control.
messages.chemical_suppressed_low_confidence: Withheld: chemical guidance requires a reliable diagnosis.
messages.chemical_advisory: Chemical control may be considered. This system does not prescribe products, doses or spray schedules. The cited sources describe the approaches below; use only products registered for this crop and disease and follow the label.
messages.no_curative_chemical: No chemical treatment cures this disease in an infected plant. Management relies on removing infected plants, preventing spread and, where relevant, controlling the vector.
messages.label_compliance: In India, use only pesticides with a CIB&RC-approved label claim for this crop and pest, and follow the label dose, interval and pre-harvest interval. Confirm with your local KVK or State Agricultural University extension service.
messages.active_ingredient_caveat: Active ingredients are listed only because the cited source names them; several sources are from outside India, and registration for this crop in India has not been verified. No dose or interval is given.
messages.expert_severe: Severe infection: consult an agricultural extension officer, KVK or plant-protection specialist before deciding on chemical control or plant removal.
messages.expert_systemic: Confirm the diagnosis with an expert (laboratory testing may be needed). Infected plants cannot be cured and may need to be removed.

monitoring: Re-inspect the plant and its neighbours every few days and note whether symptoms are spreading.
Photograph the same leaves over time to compare progression.
low_confidence: Retake the photo: a single leaf filling most of the frame, on a plain background, in even daylight without glare or strong shadows.
Avoid working among wet plants and clean hands and tools after handling affected plants, since many pathogens spread this way.
Ask an agricultural extension officer or KVK to confirm the diagnosis before any treatment.
unknown_disease: Do not apply any treatment until the problem is identified.
Take a sample of affected leaves to a local extension officer, KVK or plant clinic.
severe_removal: Remove heavily infected leaves or plants and take them out of the field (destroy them away from the crop) so they do not keep spreading the infection.
Clean tools and hands after handling infected material.

symptoms: Superficial, velvety, dark olive-green to black spots on leaves (and fruit)
Lesions first seen on the lower leaf surface, olive green with indistinct margins; they darken and become more sharply defined with age
Heavily infected leaves may become distorted and drop early
cultural_practices: Rake up and destroy fallen leaves under apple and crabapple trees in autumn, because the fungus overwinters in dead leaves
Chopping fallen leaves with a mulching mower is acceptable if combined with a urea application to fall foliage (Ohio State)
A fall foliar application of zinc sulfate and urea hastens leaf fall and decomposition, reducing overwintering inoculum (UC IPM)
Choose a suitable site, space trees for air movement, and prune annually (Ohio State)
preventive_practices: Plant scab-resistant cultivars; Ohio State calls resistance the ideal management approach and lists cultivars with complete resistance (e.g. Enterprise, Freedom, Goldrush, Liberty, Pristine, Williams Pride)
Focus control on preventing primary spring infections; risk depends on leaf-wetness periods and temperature
Ornamental crabapples are also hosts and can harbour the disease

mild: Rake up and destroy fallen leaves in autumn, because the fungus overwinters in dead leaves (UC IPM; Ohio State).
Prune annually and keep trees spaced for air movement so leaves dry quickly (Ohio State).
moderate: Where resistant cultivars are not grown, a protective fungicide programme timed to leaf-wetness periods is the primary control (Ohio State; UC IPM).
Rotate fungicide modes of action to manage resistance (UC IPM).
Continue leaf-litter sanitation to reduce next season's primary infections (UC IPM; Ohio State).
severe: Heavily infected leaves may distort and drop early; collect and destroy fallen leaves (Ohio State; UC IPM).
Plan for scab-resistant cultivars when replanting; Ohio State calls resistance the ideal management approach.

generic_guidance: Where resistant cultivars are not grown, fungicides are the primary control method (Ohio State)
Protective fungicides are applied from green tip onward, or timed by monitoring wetness periods (UC IPM)
Choose products by effectiveness, timing and mode of action, and rotate modes of action to manage fungicide resistance (UC IPM)
Protectant fungicides used by backyard growers generally need re-application after heavy rain (Ohio State)
Organic options mentioned include lime sulfur, sulfur and approved fixed-copper products (UC IPM)
Always read and follow the product label

Apple___Black_rot.pathogen: Botryosphaeria obtusa (Penn State lists it as Diplodia seriata, syn. B. obtusa)
symptoms: Leaf phase is called frogeye leaf spot: small purple specks or spots on upper leaf surfaces that enlarge into circular spots
Spots keep a purple margin while the centre turns brown, tan, yellowish-brown or light grey, giving a 'frogeye' look
Small black fruiting bodies (pycnidia) may form in the centres of older spots
Severe leaf infection can cause premature leaf drop
cultural_practices: Sanitation is the primary means of control: prune out cankers, dead branches and twigs, and remove dead wood from the orchard
Remove all mummified fruit from trees
Remove piles of prunings from the orchard perimeter or burn them (or chop them with a flail mower), because they are a major inoculum source (Ohio State)
Control fire blight by pruning out infected shoots and wood (Penn State; Ohio State)
preventive_practices: Keep trees healthy and vigorous and avoid tree stress; Ohio State calls this critical for controlling the canker phase
Prune annually and follow a balanced fertility programme based on soil and foliar analysis (Ohio State)
Neither source recommends resistant cultivars; Ohio State states all apple varieties appear equally susceptible to the fruit-rot phase

mild: Sanitation is the primary control: remove mummified fruit and dead wood from the tree (Ohio State; Penn State).
Keep trees vigorous and avoid stress (Ohio State).
moderate: Prune out cankers, dead branches and twigs, and remove pruning piles from the orchard perimeter (Ohio State).
Fungicides combined with good sanitation help control the fruit-rot phase (Ohio State; Penn State).
severe: Remove all mummified fruit and cankered wood; fungicides are not effective against the canker phase on weakened trees (Ohio State).
Control fire blight by pruning out infected shoots, because it creates entry points (Penn State; Ohio State).

generic_guidance: Fungicides combined with good sanitation help control the fruit-rot phase
Fungicides are not effective against the canker phase on weakened trees (Ohio State)
Captan and strobilurin-containing (FRAC Group 11) fungicides are effective against black rot on fruit (Penn State)

symptoms: Small yellow (chlorotic) spots on apple leaves after spring infection
Spots turn yellow-orange to orange, swell, and develop a red border or ring
Tiny black dots (spermagonia) form in the centre of the lesion on the upper surface
By mid-summer, cup-like or tube-like structures (aecia) form on the undersides of mature lesions
cultural_practices: Remove galls from junipers before the orange telial horns form (Illinois)
Ohio State cautions that removing galls from a few trees will not reduce disease in an orchard when junipers are plentiful nearby
Ohio State says removing junipers or redcedars is no longer recommended, because it only works if the primary host is removed completely
Avoid planting junipers near an apple orchard (Ohio State)
preventive_practices: Buy or plant rust-resistant apple and crabapple cultivars (Illinois; Ohio State lists resistant crabapple cultivars)
Where junipers are planted, choose rust-resistant juniper species or cultivars (Ohio State lists them)
The fungus needs both a juniper or eastern redcedar host and an apple or crabapple host to complete its life cycle

mild: The fungus needs both a juniper/red-cedar host and an apple host to complete its life cycle; note junipers nearby (Ohio State).
Avoid planting junipers near apple trees (Ohio State).
moderate: Fungicides are often part of an apple disease programme; Ohio State names sterol-inhibitor fungicides as the most effective class (Ohio State; Illinois Extension).
Removing galls from junipers before the orange telial horns form can reduce inoculum on small properties (Illinois Extension).
severe: Plan for rust-resistant apple/crabapple cultivars (Illinois Extension; Ohio State).
Note: Ohio State advises that removing junipers is no longer recommended and that gall removal has limited value where junipers are plentiful.

generic_guidance: Check with a local Extension office or garden centre for recommended fungicides (Illinois)
Fungicides are often part of an apple disease programme (Ohio State)
Ohio State names sterol-inhibitor fungicides as the most effective class against cedar-apple rust
Always follow the label

Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.pathogen: Podosphaera clandestina (UC IPM); Utah State uses Podosphaera cerasi and says it was previously misidentified as P. clandestina
symptoms: Superficial, white, weblike growth on leaves, shoots or fruit (UC IPM)
Small circular leaf lesions, lighter green than the rest of the leaf; infected parts may curl slightly (USU)
Puckered, distorted, brittle leaves, with bronzed or necrotic areas later (USU)
cultural_practices: Remove root suckers in spring; their succulent foliage is highly susceptible (USU)
Thin dense canopies by pruning out unnecessary limbs where feasible (USU)
Keep tree height manageable so the sprayer can reach the canopy (USU)
Do not over-fertilize, to avoid excess vigour (USU)
preventive_practices: Some sweet cherry cultivars have some resistance (USU names Chelan, PMR-1, Hedelfingen, Regina, Venus); Montmorency tart cherry is highly susceptible and no resistant tart cherry is available
From early to mid-May, monitor leaves on suckers and on spurs in the lowest part of the crown (USU)
Disease is worst on new growth and in years with low rainfall, high humidity and warm temperatures (UC IPM)

mild: Monitor leaves on root suckers and on spurs in the lowest part of the crown (Utah State).
Remove root suckers, whose succulent foliage is highly susceptible (Utah State).
moderate: Chemical control is the primary means of management and early-season applications matter most (Utah State); treat promptly if mildew is found on inner scaffolds or water sprouts (UC IPM).
Thin dense canopies by pruning and avoid over-fertilising (Utah State).
severe: Late in the season, once chasmothecia form, fungicides are no longer effective (Utah State); focus on sanitation and planning next season's early protection.
Rotate fungicide mode-of-action groups to limit resistance (UC IPM; Utah State).

generic_guidance: Chemical control is the primary means of management; early-season application matters most (USU)
Apply protective sprays starting soon after petal fall to protect fruit (UC IPM)
Treat immediately if mildew is found on leaves or shoots of inner scaffolds or water sprouts (UC IPM)
Sprays should target new foliage rather than the entire canopy (USU)
Rotate fungicides with different mode-of-action groups and avoid repeated use of chemically similar products, to limit resistance (UC IPM; USU)
In orchards with a history of mildew, select fungicides also active against brown rot and Botrytis (UC IPM)
Observe label pre-harvest restrictions

Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.pathogen: Cercospora zeae-maydis (CPN; UNL spells it Cercospora zea-maydis)
symptoms: Lesions appear first on the lower leaves
Long, narrow, rectangular lesions, light tan at first and later grey, bounded by leaf veins
Lesions can merge and kill entire leaves
Immature lesions can be confused with eyespot and anthracnose (UNL)
cultural_practices: The fungus survives in corn residue, so disease is often worse in corn planted after corn
Rotate to crops other than corn (UNL suggests at least one year in low-risk fields)
Tillage that buries residue and speeds its decomposition reduces fungal survival and risk
preventive_practices: Plant resistant or tolerant hybrids; UNL calls hybrid resistance the best option
Warm, humid weather favours infection, and disease severity depends on hybrid susceptibility and weather

mild: Lesions start on lower leaves; scout upward through the canopy (CPN).
Warm, humid weather favours infection; watch the crop during such spells (CPN; UNL).
moderate: Under high disease pressure, well-timed foliar fungicide applications can greatly limit yield impact (UNL).
Plan rotation away from corn, since the fungus survives in corn residue (CPN; UNL).
severe: Lesions can merge and kill entire leaves (CPN); consult an expert on whether a fungicide is still economically justified.
Bury or manage residue by tillage after harvest and use resistant hybrids next season (CPN; UNL).

generic_guidance: Foliar fungicides labeled for gray leaf spot are available (CPN)
Under high disease pressure, well-timed fungicide applications can greatly limit yield impact (UNL)

symptoms: Chlorotic flecks on the leaf that develop into powdery, brick-red (golden-brown to cinnamon-brown) pustules
Oval to elongated pustules, sparse or clustered, on both leaf surfaces
Pustules turn black as the spores mature; surrounding tissue may yellow or die, and severe infection can kill leaves
Husks, leaf sheaths and stalks can also be infected
cultural_practices: Use furrow or drip irrigation instead of overhead sprinklers, since overhead watering and high humidity favour the disease (UC IPM, home garden)
preventive_practices: Resistant hybrids and inbreds are available (CPN); some resistant varieties may be available for home gardens (UC IPM)
Disease is favoured by cool-to-moderate temperatures and high humidity; CPN says it occurs every season but is seldom a concern in hybrid field corn, and is usually more severe on seed corn

mild: Common rust occurs every season but is seldom a concern in hybrid field corn (CPN).
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation in gardens (UC IPM home garden).
moderate: Foliar fungicides labelled for common rust are available (CPN); they are generally not needed in home gardens (UC IPM).
Disease is favoured by cool-to-moderate temperatures and high humidity (CPN).
severe: Severe infection can kill leaves (CPN); consult an expert, especially for seed-corn production where the disease is usually more severe.
Use resistant hybrids in future plantings (CPN).

generic_guidance: Foliar fungicides labeled for common rust are available (CPN)
Fungicides are generally not needed in home gardens (UC IPM)

Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.pathogen: Setosphaeria turcica (named by CPN); Exserohilum turcicum (named by UT Crops)
symptoms: Long, elliptical or cigar-shaped leaf lesions, grey-green at first, then pale grey or tan
Under moist conditions, dark grey spores form, mostly on the lower leaf surface, giving lesions a 'dirty' grey look
Mature lesions are tan with distinct dark zones of sporulation (UT)
On hybrids carrying an Ht resistance gene, lesions are smaller and chlorotic and often become linear streaks (CPN)
cultural_practices: The fungus overwinters in corn residue
Crop rotation and reducing surface residue by tillage can decrease inoculum (CPN)
preventive_practices: Grow resistant hybrids where the disease is a potential problem (CPN; UT)
Ht-gene (single-gene) resistance can be overcome by some pathogen races; polygenic resistance works against all races but is less complete (CPN)
Disease is most damaging with long dew periods and moderate temperatures (UT)

mild: Monitor lesion development, especially during long dew periods and moderate temperatures (UT Crops).
moderate: Foliar fungicides may be applied when lesions are first found, where practical; several are labelled for this disease (UT Crops; CPN).
Plan crop rotation and residue reduction by tillage, since the fungus overwinters in corn residue (CPN).
severe: Consult an expert on fungicide use and yield impact.
Grow resistant hybrids where the disease is a recurring problem (CPN; UT Crops).

generic_guidance: Several foliar fungicides are labeled for northern corn leaf blight (CPN)
Foliar fungicides may be applied when lesions are first found, where practical (UT)

symptoms: Reddish-brown, circular spots on the upper leaf surface (Penn State)
Spots begin as tiny yellow spots that grow to about 1/4 inch, with rusty-red centres (Iowa State)
Tiny black dots (pycnidia) form within the leaf spots
Infected berries turn dark brown and become covered with black pycnidia, eventually forming mummies
cultural_practices: Remove infected prunings and mummified berries, and burn or bury them before new growth begins in spring; the fungus overwinters in mummies and cane lesions
Prune and destroy diseased material while vines are dormant (Iowa State)
Rake up fallen berries under the vines in autumn (Iowa State)
Remove wild grapes nearby, because they can harbour the disease (Iowa State)
preventive_practices: Planting resistant varieties is strongly suggested (Penn State)
Promote canopy drying through pruning, training, row orientation and proper spacing (Iowa State)

mild: Remove mummified berries and infected prunings, because the fungus overwinters in them (Penn State; Iowa State).
Promote canopy drying through pruning and training (Iowa State).
moderate: Early-season preventive fungicide sprays are recommended where varieties are susceptible or black rot occurred the previous year (Penn State; Iowa State).
Remove wild grapes nearby, which can harbour the disease (Iowa State).
severe: Protecting fruit late in the season is very difficult once infections are numerous (Penn State); prioritise thorough sanitation during dormancy.
Rake up fallen berries in autumn and prune out diseased material while vines are dormant (Iowa State).

generic_guidance: Where varieties are susceptible or black rot was a problem the previous year, time early-season fungicide sprays to prevent the earliest infections (Penn State)
Protecting fruit late in the season is very difficult once infections are numerous (Penn State)
In vineyards with past problems, Iowa State suggests a delayed-dormant spray (just before bud break) followed by a programme of preventive fungicide sprays

Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).pathogen: Complex of wood-infecting fungi: Phaeomoniella chlamydospora, Phaeoacremonium aleophilum (sexual stage Togninia minima) and other Phaeoacremonium spp.
symptoms: Interveinal 'tiger-stripe' discoloration on leaves, dark red in red cultivars and yellow in white cultivars, which then dries and becomes necrotic
Leaf symptoms are most common in mid-summer (UC IPM names July-August, California)
Mild symptoms can be confused with other diseases or nutritional deficiencies (FAMU)
Associated signs: small dark spots with a brown-purple ring on berries, and concentric rings of dark spots in cross-sections of canes, spurs, cordons or trunks
cultural_practices: Remove infected fruit before harvest and cultivate the vineyard to bury diseased tissue (FAMU)
UC IPM refers growers to its Eutypa dieback page for trunk-disease management practices (not fetched here)
preventive_practices: Protect pruning wounds from fungal infection so the fungi cannot colonize fresh wounds (FAMU)
Dormant pruning wounds are the infection sites and remain susceptible for several weeks after pruning, with susceptibility declining over time (UC IPM)
management: Established wood infections cannot be eradicated with fungicides (UC IPM); management focuses on protecting fresh pruning wounds (FAMU).
Remove infected fruit before harvest and bury diseased tissue by cultivation (FAMU).
Mild leaf symptoms can be confused with other diseases or nutrient deficiencies; confirm the diagnosis (FAMU).

generic_guidance: Once a pruning wound is infected, the wood infection is permanent and localized and cannot be eradicated with fungicides (UC IPM)
There are presently no effective management strategies for black measles (FAMU)
Management therefore focuses on protecting fresh pruning wounds (FAMU), because established wood infections cannot be eradicated (UC IPM)

Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.pathogen: Pseudocercospora vitis (formerly called Isariopsis leaf spot)
symptoms: Large, irregularly shaped leaf spots, dull red to brown at first (FAMU)
Spots turn black and brittle with age (FAMU)
Most common late in the season, on poorly sprayed vines (FAMU)
cultural_practices: Increase air circulation so tissues dry faster, through pruning, thinning, spacing and weed management (Kentucky, general advice for grape leaf spots)
Promote vine vigour (Kentucky)

severe: Defoliation of older leaves can be severe (UC IPM); consult an expert on whether sprays are still worthwhile.
After the crop, remove and destroy infected debris and rotate with a non-host crop (UC IPM).

generic_guidance: Copper-containing bactericides give only partial control
Copper is strictly a protectant and must be applied before an infection period occurs
Copper resistance has been observed in the pathogen; combining copper with mancozeb can partly overcome it
Some copper formulations are acceptable for certified organic production
TNAU's integrated management lists a Streptocycline spray alongside disease-free seed

UF/IFAS EDIS PP362 (fetched for the pepper entry) says that in tomato X. euvesicatoria is 'just one of four species that cause bacterial spot'. TNAU gives a Streptocycline concentration and per-acre amount; we left both out as instructed. UC IPM's spray interval and rate table were also left out.

symptoms: Brown to black leaf spots with concentric rings (bull's-eye / target pattern), often with a yellow margin
Leaf spots are leathery and usually appear on older (lower) leaves first
Stem lesions may occur; fruit infected near the calyx/stem end show sunken, dry lesions with concentric rings
cultural_practices: Remove and destroy crop debris (fungus survives on infected plant debris)
Practise crop rotation so infected debris decomposes
Destroy nightshade weeds and volunteer tomato and potato plants
preventive_practices: Seed treatment with the biocontrol agent Trichoderma asperellum (TNAU)
Be aware that infected seed is a primary source of spread (TNAU); spores spread by wind and splashing water
Disease favoured by warm, humid, rainy weather; free moisture needed for infection, development stops in hot dry weather

mild: Destroy nightshade weeds and volunteer tomato/potato plants (UC IPM).
Monitor older (lower) leaves, where spots appear first (TNAU; UC IPM).
moderate: Apply a fungicide when conditions favour disease and the first signs appear (UC IPM); TNAU lists several protectant and systemic options.
Alternate fungicides with different FRAC mode-of-action groups (UC IPM).
severe: Consult an expert on fungicide choice and timing.
After harvest, remove and destroy crop debris and rotate crops (TNAU; UC IPM).

generic_guidance: Apply a fungicide when conditions favour disease and the first signs appear (UC IPM)
Alternate fungicides with different FRAC mode-of-action groups to manage resistance
Some fixed-copper and Bacillus subtilis products are acceptable for organic production (UC IPM)
TNAU lists several protectant and systemic fungicide options for spraying

Tomato___Early_blight.research_notes: UC IPM says most California varieties are susceptible, though treatment there is rarely needed. TNAU's fungicide list gives per-acre doses and the Trichoderma seed rate; we left these out. Some TNAU entries are combination products (e.g. azoxystrobin + difenoconazole, metiram + pyraclostrobin, tebuconazole + trifloxystrobin).

symptoms: Small water-soaked leaf areas that rapidly enlarge into purple-brown to black, oily-looking blotches
Greyish-white sporulation (mycelium) on the leaf underside around lesions, especially in humid weather
Whole leaves die quickly; lesions spread to petioles and young stems
Fruit develop dark brown, firm lesions (often on shoulders) that can progress to rot
cultural_practices: Remove nearby volunteer tomato and potato plants and nightshades
Provide proper drainage
Practise crop rotation
Avoid sprinkler irrigation where possible because it favours late blight
Disc tomato fields in fall to eliminate the winter reservoir of the pathogen
preventive_practices: Grow varieties resistant to certain races of the pathogen where the disease occurs regularly
Check transplants to make sure they are free of late blight before planting
Soil application of Trichoderma asperellum (viride) is part of TNAU's integrated management
Disease is favoured by cool nights, warm/mild days and extended wet conditions from rain or fog with high humidity

mild: Late blight is favoured by cool nights and extended wet, humid conditions; inspect the crop frequently (UC IPM; TNAU).
Remove nearby volunteer tomato and potato plants and nightshades (UC IPM).
Avoid sprinkler irrigation where possible (UC IPM).
moderate: Protectant fungicides work best before disease develops; once an outbreak occurs, additional applications are needed with thorough coverage (UC IPM).
Rotate fungicide mode-of-action (FRAC) groups; mefenoxam-resistant strains have been reported (UC IPM).
severe: Whole leaves die quickly once lesions spread to petioles and stems (UC IPM; TNAU); consult an expert immediately.
After the crop, disc the field to eliminate the pathogen reservoir and practise crop rotation (UC IPM; TNAU).

generic_guidance: Apply a protectant fungicide before disease develops; once an outbreak occurs, additional applications are needed
Coverage must be thorough for fungicide applications to work
Fungicides are generally needed only when the disease appears in a rainy period or under overhead irrigation (UC IPM)
Mefenoxam-resistant strains are widespread in California, and mefenoxam is no longer effective there (UC IPM)
Rotate fungicide mode-of-action (FRAC) groups for resistance management

Tomato___Late_blight.research_notes: UC IPM calls P. infestans a 'fungus' in places; it is listed here as an oomycete (TNAU describes oomycete features: coenocytic hyphae, biflagellate zoospores, oospores). Both sources list per-acre rates, PHI/REI and spray intervals; we left these out.

symptoms: Pale green to yellowish spots on the upper leaf surface, starting on lower (older) leaves and moving up
Velvety olive-green to brown mould (conidia) on the lower leaf surface beneath the spots
Spots become necrotic; leaves wither, die and drop; severe cases can affect blossoms and fruit
Can be confused with magnesium deficiency and with early stages of other diseases
cultural_practices: Improve air circulation: adequate spacing, staking/trellising, pruning excess branches and dead leaves
Reduce humidity in greenhouses/high tunnels with fans and ventilation; avoid overhead watering; keep greenhouse night temperature above outside temperature to cut condensation
Remove and destroy infected plants (and surrounding plants in greenhouses) promptly; sanitize tools, equipment and structures between seasons
Rotate crops and move high tunnels regularly
preventive_practices: Plant resistant/tolerant varieties (both sources list cultivars)
Use clean seed from a reputable source (pathogen can survive on debris and possibly seed)
Disease is favoured by relative humidity above about 85%; mainly a problem in greenhouses and high tunnels

mild: Improve air circulation through spacing, staking and pruning excess branches and dead leaves (Cornell; UConn).
Reduce humidity in greenhouses/tunnels with ventilation; avoid overhead watering (Cornell; UConn).
moderate: Consult regional vegetable management guidelines for labelled products (UConn; Cornell).
The disease is favoured by relative humidity above about 85% (cited sources); ventilation that lowers humidity helps.
severe: Remove and destroy infected plants promptly, and in greenhouses surrounding plants too (UConn).
Sanitise tools, equipment and structures between seasons; plant resistant varieties next time (Cornell; UConn).

generic_guidance: Consult regional vegetable management guidelines for labelled products (UConn refers to the New England Vegetable Management Guide; Cornell to its Integrated Crop and Pest Management Guidelines)
Cornell reports that copper- and rhamnolipid-based organic products (Champ 30 WG, Zonix) gave the best control in its 2017-2018 organic trials
Conventional options named by Cornell include an azoxystrobin + difenoconazole product and a chlorothalonil product

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.research_notes: There is no TNAU page for tomato leaf mold. University of Minnesota Extension pages returned HTTP 403 and were dropped. Cornell names products (Champ 30 WG, Zonix, Quadris Top, Bravo Weather Stik); only the active ingredients Cornell spells out are listed. Cornell says the fungus favours 'humid, dry conditions', which is odd wording. The cultivar lists on both pages were not copied.

symptoms: Numerous small, round to irregular spots with grey/light-tan to white centres and dark margins, mostly on older (lower) leaves
Tiny black fruiting bodies (pycnidia) visible in the centre of older lesions
Spots coalesce, leaves yellow, brown and wither; rapid defoliation if untreated
Stems and flowers may also be affected
cultural_practices: Remove and destroy affected plant parts; remove infected leaves as they appear in small plantings
At season end remove as much tomato debris as possible and till in fall to break up remaining debris
Rotate away from tomatoes and potatoes (ISU suggests 3-4 years)
Where long rotation is not feasible, use an organic mulch layer after transplanting as a barrier to spore release
Improve air movement through spacing, sucker pruning and trellising; reduce overhead watering
preventive_practices: Seed treatment with the biocontrol agent Trichoderma asperellum (TNAU)
Good garden sanitation to cut overwintering inoculum on infected debris
Disease is favoured by high humidity; spores spread by rain splash or wind

mild: Remove infected leaves as they appear in small plantings (Iowa State).
Improve air movement through spacing, sucker pruning and trellising; reduce overhead watering (Iowa State).
moderate: Fungicide sprays are likely needed once the disease is present, but are seldom effective alone without other management tactics (Iowa State).
Use an organic mulch layer as a barrier to spore splash where long rotation is not feasible (Iowa State).
severe: Spots coalesce and cause rapid defoliation if untreated (TNAU); consult an expert.
At season end remove as much tomato debris as possible and rotate away from tomatoes and potatoes for 3-4 years (Iowa State).

generic_guidance: Fungicide sprays are likely needed once the disease is present; many products are labelled
Fungicides are seldom effective alone without other management tactics (ISU)
Often only preventative application is effective; read and follow all label directions

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.research_notes: TNAU gives a per-hectare dose for fluxapyroxad + pyraclostrobin and a Trichoderma seed rate; we left both out. The Iowa State page is written for home gardens.

symptoms: Fine white-to-yellow stippling/speckling on leaves from sap feeding, often mottled
Leaves bronze, turn reddish-brown or brown, dry up and may curl; yellowing and leaf drop can expose fruit to sunscald
Silken webbing on leaf undersides under heavy infestations
Flower and fruit formation can be affected under severe infestation (TNAU)
cultural_practices: Inspect new plants regularly before bringing them into a growing area
Scout leaf undersides with a hand lens, or shake plants over white paper to detect mites
Physically spray plants with high-pressure water to dislodge mites
preventive_practices: Encourage natural enemies such as lady beetles (Stethorus spp.), lacewings and predatory thrips
Be aware that warm, dry conditions (and protected structures that limit rain splash) favour rapid mite reproduction

mild: Scout leaf undersides with a hand lens, or shake plants over white paper (UConn).
Spray plants with high-pressure water to dislodge mites (UConn).
moderate: Insecticidal soaps and horticultural oils are effective with minimal impact on beneficials but need direct contact and repeat applications (UConn).
Encourage natural enemies such as lady beetles, lacewings and predatory thrips (UConn).
severe: Use miticides (not fungicides) with thorough coverage of leaf undersides, rotating modes of action to prevent resistance (UConn); consult an expert on product choice.
Warm, dry conditions favour rapid mite build-up; act quickly (UConn).

generic_guidance: Use miticides with thorough coverage of leaf undersides
Rotate miticides with different modes of action to prevent resistance
Insecticidal soaps and horticultural oils are effective with minimal impact on beneficials but need direct contact and repeat applications
Consult regional vegetable management guides for crop-specific products
chemical_guidance.note: This is a mite pest: miticides/acaricides apply, not fungicides.

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.research_notes: This is an arachnid pest, not a pathogen; the 'pathogen' field holds the pest name. The UConn page names Tetranychus urticae. The TNAU page covers 'Red spider mite: Tetranychus spp' on tomato at genus level and does not name T. urticae; its only control is wettable sulphur, and we left out the rate. An earlier search snippet said this TNAU page also mentions dicofol; the fetched page does not, so dicofol is not listed. UC IPM's tomato guidelines have no spider-mite page (we checked the index).

symptoms: Leaf lesions begin as dark brown pinpoint spots, nearly identical to early bacterial spot
Lesions enlarge with light brown to grey centres and dark concentric rings, sometimes with diffuse yellowing; easily confused with early blight or gray leaf spot
Lesions coalesce, causing blighting and premature defoliation; disease often starts in the inner canopy
Petiole/stem lesions dark brown and oval; fruit get sunken, pitted lesions that may crack in an 'X' or star pattern
cultural_practices: Rotate tomato fields with non-solanaceous crops
Eliminate weeds (especially Solanaceae), volunteers and plant debris that harbour inoculum
preventive_practices: Start with clean, healthy transplants
No commercial tomato varieties with resistance to target spot are currently available; varietal differences are only degrees of susceptibility
Disease is favoured by warm temperatures, high humidity and prolonged leaf wetness; a dense canopy holds moisture

mild: Disease often starts in the inner canopy and is favoured by prolonged leaf wetness; avoid dense canopies (UF/IFAS).
Eliminate solanaceous weeds and volunteers that harbour inoculum (UF/IFAS).
moderate: With no resistant varieties available, routine protective fungicides are the main control in Florida (UF/IFAS); reduced efficacy of QoI and variable SDHI control have been reported, so rotate modes of action.
severe: Even effective fungicides may struggle when weather strongly favours the disease (UF/IFAS); consult an expert.
Rotate tomato fields with non-solanaceous crops and remove plant debris (UF/IFAS).

generic_guidance: With no host resistance available, routine application of protective fungicides is the main control in Florida; significant losses are expected without fungicides
Even effective fungicides may struggle when weather strongly favours the disease
Reduced efficacy of the QoI (FRAC 11) fungicide azoxystrobin has been reported, and control with QoI and SDHI (FRAC 7) fungicides varies
Loss of SDHI fungicides to resistance would seriously hamper management; fungicide-resistant isolates may carry over between seasons
Biopesticides are listed in the Vegetable Production Handbook of Florida

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.pathogen: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus (TYLCV), a geminivirus (family Geminiviridae)
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.vector: Whitefly Bemisia tabaci (sweetpotato/silverleaf whitefly, B. tabaci MEAM1; MED also present in Florida)
symptoms: Stunted, erect/upright growth; plants infected early are severely stunted
Small leaves that curl upward with strong crumpling and interveinal and marginal yellowing (bright yellow leaf margins)
Shortened internodes giving a bushy appearance; flowers often drop and fruit yield falls sharply
cultural_practices: Rogue (remove) diseased plants while incidence is low
Practise good weed management in and around fields (weeds such as nightshade and jimsonweed can be hosts)
Promptly destroy harvested tomato fields, old crop residue and volunteers; UF calls this the most effective way to cut whitefly numbers and virus inoculum
Use a regional host-free period where there is no true winter
Avoid planting new fields near older (especially infected) fields
preventive_practices: Select TYLCV-resistant/tolerant varieties (UF notes tolerant varieties can still be infected and lose yield under high virus pressure)
Use virus- and whitefly-free transplants; do not import transplants from areas known to have the virus
Cover plants with fine-mesh floating row covers to exclude whiteflies
Metalized (reflective) plastic mulch can repel whiteflies and reduce early-season transmission
Plant right after a tomato-free period or a true winter season
management: Rogue (remove) diseased plants while incidence is low (UC IPM; UF/IFAS).
Promptly destroy old crops, crop residue and volunteers after harvest; UF/IFAS calls this the most effective way to cut whitefly numbers and virus inoculum.
Avoid planting new fields near older, infected fields (UF/IFAS).
vector_management: Management targets the whitefly vector Bemisia tabaci, not the virus (UC IPM; UF/IFAS).
Use fine-mesh row covers and reflective mulch to reduce early-season transmission (UC IPM; UF/IFAS).
Whiteflies have developed resistance to several insecticides; rotate modes of action and spray only when needed (UF/IFAS).

generic_guidance: No chemical treatment for the virus itself is given; management targets the whitefly vector
Systemic insecticides (e.g. IRAC Group 4 neonicotinoids/butenolides, Group 28 diamides) are key whitefly tools; translaminar and contact products are also used
Whiteflies (B. tabaci) have developed resistance to several insecticides (e.g. imidacloprid, thiamethoxam, spirotetramat in Florida); rotate modes of action and spray only when needed
Biopesticides such as insecticidal soap and mineral oil can help suppress whiteflies; kaolin clay gave variable results

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.pathogen: Tomato mosaic virus (ToMV), a tobamovirus (UC IPM covers it together with Tobacco mosaic virus)
symptoms: Mild mosaic / green mottling on leaves, sometimes curled, stunted or slightly deformed
Leaf malformation including a fern-like appearance; shoestring-like leaves can occur in cool weather
Plants often stunted and somewhat yellowed; necrotic patterns may develop on fruit
cultural_practices: Extreme sanitation is needed; the viruses are easily transmitted mechanically by hands, tools, clothing and equipment
Immediately remove and destroy infected plants
Wash hands frequently with soap and water when handling plants; do not handle plants after using tobacco products
Be aware that tobamoviruses are very stable and can survive in plant debris for years
preventive_practices: Use seed treated to eliminate seedborne inoculum
Grow cultivars with genetic resistance to specific tomato-infecting tobamoviruses
Be aware that infections are common in transplants and handled/trained plants and seldom seen in direct-seeded fields (UC IPM)
management: Immediately remove and destroy infected plants (UC IPM; WSU).
Extreme sanitation is required: the virus spreads mechanically on hands, tools, clothing and equipment (UC IPM).
Wash hands with soap and water when handling plants; do not handle plants after using tobacco products (UC IPM; WSU).
vector_management: Tobamoviruses have no insect vector, so insecticides are not part of control (UC IPM).

generic_guidance: No chemical management is recommended (WSU)
Tobamoviruses have no insect, nematode or fungal vectors, so insecticides are not part of control (UC IPM)

Avoid overhead irrigation and give plants space and support for air movement (UC IPM; Iowa State).

Scout regularly, checking older leaves and leaf undersides (UC IPM; UConn).
